claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among the constituent elements enhances lattice distortion in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced lattice distortion produces local internal elastic strain fields.
Internal elastic strain lowers cohesive energy at or near the nanoparticle surface.
Lower surface cohesive energy reduces the energetic barrier to forming a liquid-like premelted layer.
Greater atomic size mismatch therefore lowers the premelting onset temperature relative to an alloy with minimal mismatch.
The baseline nanoparticles are equimolar CoCrFeMnNi.
The baseline nanoparticles are synthesized by ultrafast laser ablation.
The nanoparticles have diameters in the range of 3–10 nm.
The baseline CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles crystallize as a single solid-solution phase.
Equimolar CoCrFeMnNi has minimally mismatched atomic radii and correspondingly low lattice distortion and internal strain.
Substituting species with elements having larger or smaller atomic radii can incrementally increase atomic size mismatch.
The controlled comparison should vary atomic size mismatch while holding nanoparticle size and synthesis conditions constant.
Higher-mismatch nanoparticles are expected to have a lower premelting onset temperature than the equimolar baseline.
Higher-mismatch nanoparticles may exhibit a broader premelting temperature regime than the equimolar baseline.
The proposed mismatch-controlled mechanism should hold for 3–10 nm nanoparticles under inert conditions.
The mechanism is conditioned on retention of a single-phase solid solution without phase segregation or gross compositional inhomogeneity.
Secondary phases would confound attribution of altered melting behavior to lattice distortion.
Differential scanning calorimetry can determine the premelting onset temperature and melting thermal signature in these nanoparticles.
In situ TEM can visually detect liquid-like surface layers and premelted regions during thermal ramping.
High-resolution XRD or atom-probe tomography can establish whether the samples retain a single solid-solution phase without significant secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The boundary and predicted-outcome fields treat secondary-phase formation as a confounder that places a sample outside the proposed single-phase mechanism, whereas the falsification rule treats detection of secondary phases correlated with melting behavior as falsification of that mechanism. A violated scope condition invalidates the controlled test rather than directly falsifying the stated mismatch mechanism.

The central hypothesis specifically predicts a lower premelting onset, while broadening is described only as potential. The parenthetical 'or a broader temperature range' in the falsification rule could allow broadening alone to rescue a failure to observe the required onset-temperature decrease.
